# React.js Interview Preparation — Complete Revision Guide ## A Deep, First-Principles Explanation for Beginners through Senior Developers --- ## 0. How to Use This Guide This document is a complete revision guide for React.js interviews, spanning beginner to senior level. It is organized as a progression: 1. Fundamentals — what React is, JSX, components, props, state. 2. State Management — how useState really works, snapshots, immutability. 3. Hooks — the full toolbox. 4. Rendering & Lifecycle — how React turns state into pixels. 5. Virtual DOM, Reconciliation, Fiber — the engine underneath. 6. Performance — making React fast. 7. Forms, APIs, State Management — real application concerns. 8. React 19 — the newest features. 9. Advanced & Senior Scenarios — architecture, system design, tricky questions. Because you already work with React 19, Laravel, REST APIs, and enterprise ERP applications, examples lean toward realistic ERP-style scenarios (employees, salaries, dashboards). Let's begin from first principles. --- # PART 1 — REACT FUNDAMENTALS ## 1. What Is React? ### The Simple Intuition Imagine you are building a house. You don't carve the entire house out of one giant block of stone. Instead, you assemble it from bricks, doors, windows, and rooms — each reusable, each self-contained. If a window breaks, you replace the window, not the house. React applies this same idea to user interfaces. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using reusable components. It was created at Meta (formerly Facebook) to solve a specific problem: as web apps grew, manually updating the DOM (the browser's representation of the page) became error-prone and slow. React lets you describe what the UI should look like, and it figures out how to update the page efficiently. ### A Minimal Example jsx function Welcome() { return

Welcome to React

; } export default Welcome; That's it. A function that returns markup. React takes care of inserting it into the page. ### Why This Matters — The Mental Shift Before React, you wrote imperative code: step-by-step instructions telling the browser exactly what to do. javascript const heading = document.createElement("h1"); heading.textContent = "Hello World"; document.body.appendChild(heading); You created an element, set its text, and attached it. If the text changed, you'd have to find the element again and update it manually. React flips this. You write declarative code: you describe the end result, and React handles the steps. jsx function App() { return

Hello World

; } ### Imperative vs. Declarative — Why the Distinction Matters | Approach | What You Say | Analogy | |---|---|---| | Imperative |

| Giving someone turn-by-turn driving directions. |
| Declarative |

| Telling a taxi driver the destination and letting them navigate. |

Analogy connection: In a taxi, you say

You don't specify every turn. React is the driver: you describe what (destination = the UI for a given state), and React decides how (which DOM nodes to update). This is the single most important mental model in React. Everything else follows from it. ### Interview Question: Is React a Framework or a Library? React is primarily a UI library. A library gives you tools you call. A framework calls your code and dictates structure. React alone doesn't provide: - Routing (you'd add React Router). - Data fetching conventions (you'd use fetch, Axios, TanStack Query, etc.). - Backend operations (you'd use Laravel, Node, etc.). - Form management (you'd use React Hook Form, Formik). React focuses on one thing: rendering UI from state. Everything else is composable. > Senior note: This is why the React ecosystem is so large. React's narrow scope is a feature, not a bug — it lets you compose best-in-class libraries rather than accept one framework's opinions. --- ## 2. What Is JSX? ### The Simple Intuition JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. jsx const element =

Hello React

; It looks like HTML. It is not HTML. It is a syntax extension that a build tool (Babel, SWC, Vite, etc.) compiles into JavaScript. ### What JSX Actually Compiles To Traditional transformation: javascript React.createElement("h1", null, "Hello React"); Modern React uses the automatic JSX runtime, so you don't need to import React at the top of every file. But conceptually, JSX always becomes function calls that produce React elements (plain JavaScript objects describing what to render). ### Why JSX Exists Without JSX, building UI in JavaScript is verbose and disconnected from the visual result. JSX keeps markup, logic, and styling co-located — you see the structure and behavior in one place. Important: JSX is not required to use React. You can call React.createElement directly. But JSX is overwhelmingly preferred for readability. ### The Four JSX Rules #### Rule 1: Return a Single Root Element JSX expressions must have one parent. Incorrect: jsx function App() { return (

Hello

Welcome

); } Correct (using a Fragment): jsx function App() { return ( <>

Hello

Welcome

); } Why? JSX compiles to a function call that returns one value. Two sibling elements would mean returning two values — illegal in JavaScript. A Fragment (<>...) groups them without adding a DOM node. > Analogy: A function can return one envelope. If you have two letters, you put them in one envelope (fragment) — the envelope doesn't add anything visible; it just groups. #### Rule 2: Use className Instead of class jsx
Content
Why? class is a reserved word in JavaScript. JSX attributes map to JavaScript object properties, so class would conflict. React uses className (the DOM property name). #### Rule 3: Use htmlFor Instead of for jsx Why? Same reason — for is a reserved JavaScript keyword. htmlFor is the DOM property. #### Rule 4: Use Curly Braces for JavaScript Expressions jsx const name = "Ahmad"; return

Hello {name}

; Curly braces {} embed any JavaScript expression (not statements). You can put variables, function calls, ternaries, and .map() calls inside. ### Interview Question: Why Do We Use JSX? JSX makes component markup easier to understand, maintain, and combine with JavaScript expressions. It isn't strictly required, but it dramatically improves readability and developer experience. --- ## 3. React Components ### The Simple Intuition A component is a reusable building block. Think of LEGO bricks: each brick is a self-contained piece with a defined shape, and you snap them together to build anything. ### Functional Component (Standard) jsx function Employee() { return (

Employee Details

Name: Ahmad

); } ### Arrow Function Component jsx const Employee = () => { return

Employee Details

; }; Both are valid. Modern React favors function components (class components are legacy). ### Component Composition This is the heart of React architecture. You build complex UIs by combining small components. jsx function Header() { return
ERP System
; } function Sidebar() { return
Navigation
; } function Dashboard() { return
Dashboard Content
; } function App() { return ( <>
); } ### Visualizing Composition ┌─────────────┐ │ App │ └──────┬──────┘ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌─────────┐ │Header │ │Sidebar│ │Dashboard│ └───────┘ └───────┘ └─────────┘ ### Interview Question: What Is Component Composition? Composition means constructing complex interfaces by combining smaller, reusable components. Benefits: - Reusability — write once, use everywhere. - Maintainability — small, focused files are easier to change. - Separation of concerns — each component owns one job. - Testability — small units are easier to test in isolation. - Consistent design — shared components enforce visual consistency. > Senior interview point: Prefer composition over building giant components with many responsibilities. If a component handles layout, data fetching, and business logic, split it. This is the React equivalent of the Single Responsibility Principle. --- ## 4.
